# Glossary of Health and Wellbeing Systems & AI Concepts

This glossary provides definitions of key concepts in Health and Wellbeing Systems and AI, curated for the UNINOVIS alliance research context. Each entry includes revised academic references.

---

## AI and Healthcare

AI in Healthcare refers to the application of AI techniques to medical and health-related domains, including **clinical decision support**, **medical image analysis**, **drug discovery**, **patient monitoring**, and **health system optimization**.

l image analysis**, **drug discovery**, **patient monitoring**, and **health system optimization**. It has an impact in three levels: for clinicians, predominantly via rapid, accurate image interpretation; for health systems, by improving workflow and the potential for reducing medical errors; and for patients, by enabling them to process their own data to promote health. Robust clinical evaluation, using metrics that are intuitive to clinicians and ideally go beyond measures of technical accuracy to include quality of care and patient outcomes is essential.

eyond measures of technical accuracy to include quality of care and patient outcomes is essential.

Responsible AI in healthcare is particularly critical due to the relatively low data and validated proof. Because of the high stakes involved, requiring systematic debugging, extensive simulation, and rigorous validation, transparency, fairness across patient demographics, and compliance with medical regulations.

tion, transparency, fairness across patient demographics, and compliance with medical regulations.

The WHO Expert Group identified six core principles: Protect autonomy; Promote human well-being, human safety, and the public interest; Ensure transparency, explainability, and intelligibility; Foster responsibility and accountability; Ensure inclusiveness and equity; Promote AI that is responsive and sustainable.

**Related concepts:** Digital Health; Precision Medicine; Clinical Decision Support; Wellbeing Systems; Health Informatics; AI Ethics in Healthcare; Wearable Health Technology

## Wellbeing Systems

Wellbeing systems refer to integrated technological and social frameworks designed to monitor, promote, and enhance the **physical**, **mental**, and **social well-being** of individuals and communities. These systems may incorporate **wearable sensors**, **ambient intelligence**, **mobile health applications**, **social robotics**, and **AI-driven analytics** to support health maintenance, early detection of decline, and quality of life improvement.

ytics** to support health maintenance, early detection of decline, and quality of life improvement. Wellbeing systems span the continuum from prevention and health promotion to chronic disease management and assisted living.

A key principle is the **person-centred** approach, where technology serves to augment individual autonomy and quality of life rather than imposing surveillance or control. Wellbeing systems are particularly relevant in the context of **aging populations**, **mental health support**, and **community health** interventions.

ntext of **aging populations**, **mental health support**, and **community health** interventions.

**Related concepts:** AI and Healthcare; Digital Health; Aging and AI; Mental Health and AI; Wearable Health Technology; Ambient Assisted Living; Human-Centred AI

## Digital Health

Digital health encompasses the use of **information and communication technologies** (ICT) in healthcare, including **telemedicine**, **mobile health (mHealth)**, **electronic health records (EHR)**, **health information systems**, and **AI-powered health tools**.

electronic health records (EHR)**, **health information systems**, and **AI-powered health tools**. It represents the convergence of digital technologies with health, healthcare, living, and society to enhance the efficiency of healthcare delivery and make medicine more personalised and precise.

Digital health technologies have the potential to improve access to healthcare, reduce costs, enhance patient engagement, and enable continuous health monitoring.

s to healthcare, reduce costs, enhance patient engagement, and enable continuous health monitoring. However, they also raise concerns about **data privacy**, **digital divide**, **interoperability**, and **algorithmic bias** in health-related decisions.

**Related concepts:** AI and Healthcare; Health Informatics; Telemedicine and Telehealth; Wearable Health Technology; Precision Medicine; Privacy and Data Governance in Health

## Aging and AI

Aging and AI refers to the application of artificial intelligence technologies to address the challenges and opportunities associated with **aging populations**. This includes **fall detection systems**, **cognitive decline monitoring**, **social robotics for companionship**, **AI-assisted rehabilitation**, **smart home environments**, and **age-friendly technology design**.

*AI-assisted rehabilitation**, **smart home environments**, and **age-friendly technology design**. As global demographics shift toward older populations, AI-driven solutions are increasingly explored to support **independent living**, **early diagnosis of age-related conditions**, and **improved quality of life** for older adults.

Key challenges include ensuring that AI systems are **accessible** and **usable** by older adults, avoiding **ageist biases** in algorithmic design, protecting the **privacy** and **dignity** of elderly users, and addressing the **digital divide** that may exclude

*privacy** and **dignity** of elderly users, and addressing the **digital divide** that may exclude older populations from AI-enabled health services.

**Related concepts:** Wellbeing Systems; AI and Healthcare; Frailty Syndrome; Ambient Assisted Living; Wearable Health Technology; Cognitive Impairments; Neurodegenerative Disorders

## Mental Health and AI

Mental Health and AI encompasses the application of AI technologies to the **detection**, **diagnosis**, **treatment**, and **prevention** of mental health conditions. Applications include **natural language processing (NLP)** for analysing clinical notes and social media posts to detect signs of depression or suicidal ideation, **conversational AI** and **chatbots** for therapeutic support, **predictive models** for identifying at-risk individuals, and **digital phenotyping** using smartphone a

dictive models** for identifying at-risk individuals, and **digital phenotyping** using smartphone and wearable data to monitor mental health states.

Key ethical considerations include the **sensitivity of mental health data**, the risk of **over-reliance on automated tools** in clinical settings, the need for **cultural sensitivity** in AI models, and the importance of **human oversight** in mental health care decisions. There are also concerns about **algorithmic bias** in mental health assessment tools, which may perform differently across demographic groups.

bias** in mental health assessment tools, which may perform differently across demographic groups.

**Related concepts:** AI and Healthcare; Wellbeing Systems; Digital Health; Psychological Impact of AI; Cognitive Impairments; Privacy and Data Governance in Health

## Precision Medicine

Precision medicine (also called **personalised medicine**) is an approach to patient care that takes into account individual differences in patients' **genes**, **environments**, and **lifestyles** to tailor prevention and treatment strategies.

nts' **genes**, **environments**, and **lifestyles** to tailor prevention and treatment strategies. AI plays a critical role in precision medicine by enabling the analysis of large-scale **genomic data**, **electronic health records**, **medical imaging**, and **multi-omics datasets** to identify patient-specific risk profiles and optimal therapeutic interventions.

omics datasets** to identify patient-specific risk profiles and optimal therapeutic interventions.

Key applications include **pharmacogenomics** (predicting drug responses based on genetic profiles), **cancer genomics** (identifying targetable mutations), **radiomics** (extracting quantitative features from medical images), and **risk stratification** models for chronic diseases.

**Related concepts:** AI and Healthcare; Genomics; Radiomics; Clinical Decision Support; Health Informatics; Digital Health

## Clinical Decision Support

Clinical Decision Support (CDS) systems are health information technologies designed to assist clinicians, patients, and other health professionals in making informed healthcare decisions. AI-based CDS systems use **machine learning**, **knowledge bases**, **clinical guidelines**, and **patient data** to provide evidence-based recommendations, alerts, reminders, and diagnostic suggestions at the point of care.

vidence-based recommendations, alerts, reminders, and diagnostic suggestions at the point of care.

AI-enhanced CDS can improve **diagnostic accuracy**, reduce **medical errors**, support **treatment selection**, and facilitate adherence to **clinical guidelines**. However, challenges include the risk of **alert fatigue**, the need for **transparency** in algorithmic recommendations, integration with existing **clinical workflows**, and the importance of maintaining **clinician autonomy** in final decision-making.

al workflows**, and the importance of maintaining **clinician autonomy** in final decision-making.

**Related concepts:** AI and Healthcare; Health Informatics; Precision Medicine; Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI); Digital Health

## Wearable Health Technology

Wearable health technology refers to electronic devices worn on the body that collect, process, and transmit **physiological data** for health monitoring and management.

dy that collect, process, and transmit **physiological data** for health monitoring and management. These devices include **smartwatches**, **fitness trackers**, **biosensors**, **electrocardiogram (ECG) patches**, **continuous glucose monitors**, and **electrooculography** devices. Combined with AI, wearable data enables **real-time health monitoring**, **early detection of anomalies**, **fall detection**, **sleep analysis**, and **activity recognition**.

ly detection of anomalies**, **fall detection**, **sleep analysis**, and **activity recognition**.

In the context of health and wellbeing systems, wearables are essential for **remote patient monitoring**, **chronic disease management**, **elderly care**, and **preventive health**. Key challenges include **data accuracy and reliability**, **battery life**, **user compliance**, **data privacy**, and the clinical validation of wearable-derived health metrics.

er compliance**, **data privacy**, and the clinical validation of wearable-derived health metrics.

**Related concepts:** Digital Health; AI and Healthcare; Aging and AI; Automatic Fall Detection; Wellbeing Systems; Ambient Assisted Living

## Health Informatics

Health informatics (also called **biomedical informatics** or **medical informatics**) is the interdisciplinary field that studies the effective use of **data**, **information**, and **knowledge** for scientific inquiry, problem-solving, and decision-making in healthcare.

on**, and **knowledge** for scientific inquiry, problem-solving, and decision-making in healthcare. It integrates principles from **computer science**, **information science**, **cognitive science**, and **health sciences** to design, develop, and evaluate information systems and technologies that improve individual and population health outcomes.

Key areas include **electronic health records (EHR)**, **health data standards** (HL7, FHIR), **clinical natural language processing**, **public health surveillance**, **health data analytics**, and **interoperability** between health information sy

th surveillance**, **health data analytics**, and **interoperability** between health information systems.

## Neurodegenerative Disorders and AI

Neurodegenerative disorders are diseases characterised by the progressive loss of structure or function of neurons, including **Alzheimer's disease**, **Parkinson's disease**, **multiple sclerosis**, **amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)**, and **Huntington's disease**.

e**, **multiple sclerosis**, **amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)**, and **Huntington's disease**. AI is increasingly applied to these conditions for **early diagnosis** using neuroimaging (e.g., **structural brain MRI**, PET scans), **disease progression modelling**, **drug discovery**, **speech and language analysis** for cognitive assessment, and **biomarker identification** from multi-modal data.

guage analysis** for cognitive assessment, and **biomarker identification** from multi-modal data.

AI-driven approaches have shown promise in detecting subtle patterns in brain imaging data that precede clinical symptoms, enabling earlier intervention. Challenges include the need for **large, well-annotated datasets**, **model interpretability** for clinical trust, **heterogeneity** of disease manifestations, and ethical considerations around **predictive diagnosis** of incurable conditions.

anifestations, and ethical considerations around **predictive diagnosis** of incurable conditions.

## Frailty Syndrome

Frailty syndrome is a clinically recognisable state of increased vulnerability resulting from age-associated decline in reserve and function across multiple physiological systems, such that the ability to cope with everyday or acute stressors is compromised.

ysiological systems, such that the ability to cope with everyday or acute stressors is compromised. It is characterised by **reduced muscle strength**, **slow gait**, **low physical activity**, **unintentional weight loss**, and **self-reported exhaustion**. AI applications in frailty include **automated frailty assessment** from clinical data, **fall risk prediction**, **gait analysis** using sensors and computer vision, and **personalised intervention planning**.

, **gait analysis** using sensors and computer vision, and **personalised intervention planning**.

**Wearable sensors** and **ambient monitoring systems** enable continuous, non-intrusive assessment of frailty indicators in real-world settings, supporting early detection and timely interventions.

**Related concepts:** Aging and AI; AI and Healthcare; Wearable Health Technology; Automatic Fall Detection; Wellbeing Systems; Ambient Assisted Living

## Telemedicine and Telehealth

Telemedicine refers to the practice of providing **clinical healthcare services** at a distance using **telecommunications technology**, while telehealth is a broader term that also encompasses non-clinical applications such as **health education**, **administrative meetings**, and **public health surveillance**.

ions such as **health education**, **administrative meetings**, and **public health surveillance**. AI enhances telemedicine through **automated triage**, **remote diagnostic support**, **virtual health assistants**, and **AI-powered analysis of remotely collected data** (e.g., images, vital signs, audio recordings).

The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the adoption of telemedicine worldwide, highlighting both its potential to improve **access to care** (especially in rural and underserved areas) and challenges related to **digital literacy**, **connectivity**, **regulatory frameworks**, and **p

and challenges related to **digital literacy**, **connectivity**, **regulatory frameworks**, and **patient-clinician trust** in remote interactions.

## Genomics and AI

Genomics is the study of the complete set of DNA (the **genome**) of an organism, including gene interactions, gene-environment interactions, and their influence on health and disease.

luding gene interactions, gene-environment interactions, and their influence on health and disease. AI and machine learning are transforming genomics through applications in **variant classification**, **gene expression analysis**, **genome-wide association studies (GWAS)**, **protein structure prediction**, and **pharmacogenomics**. Deep learning models have achieved breakthroughs in predicting protein structures (e.g., AlphaFold) and identifying disease-associated genetic variants from sequencing data.

ctures (e.g., AlphaFold) and identifying disease-associated genetic variants from sequencing data.

Key challenges include the **interpretability** of genomic AI models, **bias** from underrepresentation of diverse populations in genomic databases, **data sharing and privacy** concerns (genomic data is inherently identifiable), and the ethical implications of **predictive genetic testing**.

**Related concepts:** Precision Medicine; AI and Healthcare; Health Informatics; Microbiome; Privacy and Data Governance in Health

## Cancer Detection and AI

AI in cancer detection refers to the use of machine learning and deep learning techniques to identify, classify, and characterise cancerous tissues and biomarkers from **medical imaging** (mammography, histopathology, CT, MRI), **laboratory data**, and **genomic profiles**. Applications include **breast cancer screening** from mammograms, **lung cancer detection** from CT scans, **skin cancer classification** from dermoscopic images, and **colorectal cancer detection** from colonoscopy video.

AI systems have demonstrated performance comparable to or exceeding that of expert radiologists and pathologists in certain diagnostic tasks. However, challenges remain in **clinical validation**, **generalisability** across populations and imaging equipment, **regulatory approval**, **integration into clinical workflows**, and ensuring that AI tools reduce rather than exacerbate **health disparities**.

## Ambient Assisted Living

Ambient Assisted Living (AAL) refers to the use of **smart environments**, **sensors**, **Internet of Things (IoT) devices**, and AI to support the daily activities and safety of individuals — particularly **older adults** and people with **disabilities** — in their living spaces.

ividuals — particularly **older adults** and people with **disabilities** — in their living spaces. AAL systems aim to enable **independent living**, improve **safety** (e.g., fall detection, activity anomaly detection), enhance **comfort**, and provide **emergency response** capabilities.

Key technologies include **motion sensors**, **smart home platforms**, **voice assistants**, **environmental sensors** (temperature, humidity, light), and **AI-based activity recognition** systems.

ironmental sensors** (temperature, humidity, light), and **AI-based activity recognition** systems. Ethical considerations include **privacy** in continuous home monitoring, **consent** (especially for cognitively impaired individuals), and avoiding a sense of **surveillance** that could undermine dignity and autonomy.

**Related concepts:** Aging and AI; Wellbeing Systems; Wearable Health Technology; Automatic Fall Detection; Frailty Syndrome; Digital Health

## AI Ethics in Healthcare

AI Ethics in Healthcare specifically addresses the moral and regulatory considerations arising from deploying AI systems in health-related contexts, where decisions directly affect human life, dignity, and wellbeing. Unlike general AI ethics, healthcare-specific ethical concerns are amplified by the **vulnerability of patients**, the **asymmetry of information** between clinicians and patients, the **life-or-death nature** of medical decisions, and the strict **regulatory environment** governing

e **life-or-death nature** of medical decisions, and the strict **regulatory environment** governing health technologies.

Core ethical principles drawn from bioethics — **beneficence**, **non-maleficence**, **autonomy**, and **justice** — are applied to evaluate AI systems in healthcare. Key issues include **informed consent** for AI-assisted diagnosis, **equitable access** to AI-enabled healthcare, **bias** in clinical AI models trained on unrepresentative data, **liability** when AI recommendations lead to adverse outcomes, and the preservation of the **therapeutic relationship** between cl

ations lead to adverse outcomes, and the preservation of the **therapeutic relationship** between clinician and patient.

**Related concepts:** AI and Healthcare; Fairness in AI; Bias in AI; Transparency in AI; Privacy and Data Governance in Health; Clinical Decision Support

## Fairness in AI

Fairness in AI concerns the design and evaluation of AI systems to ensure they do not produce bias, understood as any prejudice or favoritism towards an individual or group based on their inherent or acquired characteristics.

e or favoritism towards an individual or group based on their inherent or acquired characteristics. It is the moral lens through which we examine decisions made by AI systems that do not produce discriminatory outcomes across different groups defined by protected attributes such as race, gender, age, or disability, among other characteristics. In health and wellbeing contexts, fairness is particularly critical as **biased health AI** can lead to **misdiagnosis**, **unequal treatment recommendations**, and **health disparities** across demographic groups.

is**, **unequal treatment recommendations**, and **health disparities** across demographic groups.

**Related concepts:** Bias in AI; AI Ethics in Healthcare; Transparency in AI; Clinical Decision Support

## Bias in AI

Bias in AI refers to systematic errors or prejudices in AI system outputs that arise from biased training data, flawed model design, or biased human decisions during development.

arise from biased training data, flawed model design, or biased human decisions during development. In health and wellbeing systems, bias can manifest as **underdiagnosis in underrepresented populations**, **unequal prediction accuracy** across demographic groups, or **training data that overrepresents certain health conditions or populations**. Types of AI bias include data biases (representation, sampling, measurement bias), algorithmic biases, and deployment biases (user interaction, population bias).

measurement bias), algorithmic biases, and deployment biases (user interaction, population bias).

**Related concepts:** Fairness in AI; AI Ethics in Healthcare; Clinical Decision Support; Privacy and Data Governance in Health

## Privacy and Data Governance in Health

Privacy in health AI involves protecting **personal health information (PHI)** and **sensitive medical data** from unauthorized access and ensuring that data is used responsibly throughout the AI lifecycle.

** from unauthorized access and ensuring that data is used responsibly throughout the AI lifecycle. Health data is among the most sensitive categories of personal data, subject to strict regulations including the **General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)**, **HIPAA** (in the US), and the **EU AI Act** for AI systems processing health data.

Technical approaches to preserving privacy include **differential privacy**, **federated learning** (training models across distributed hospital data without centralising patient records), **data minimisation**, and **synthetic data generation**.

ta without centralising patient records), **data minimisation**, and **synthetic data generation**. Data governance in health defines the decision rights and accountabilities for how health data is collected, stored, processed, shared, and used for AI development.

**Related concepts:** AI Ethics in Healthcare; AI and Healthcare; Digital Health; Health Informatics; Genomics and AI

## Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)

Explainable AI (XAI) refers to methods and techniques that make the behaviour and outputs of AI systems understandable to humans. In health and wellbeing systems, XAI is critical because clinicians need to understand **why** an AI system recommends a particular diagnosis or treatment to make informed decisions and maintain **clinical accountability**. XAI aims to bridge the gap between high-performing but opaque models (such as deep neural networks) and the need for human interpretability.

rforming but opaque models (such as deep neural networks) and the need for human interpretability.

Key XAI methods include **LIME** (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), **SHAP** (SHapley Additive explanations), **attention mechanisms**, **saliency maps**, and **concept-based explanations**. In healthcare, explainability is not only a technical requirement but also a **regulatory** one: the EU AI Act classifies health-related AI systems as high-risk, requiring transparency and documentation of decision-making processes.

ed AI systems as high-risk, requiring transparency and documentation of decision-making processes.

**Related concepts:** AI Ethics in Healthcare; Transparency in AI; Clinical Decision Support; AI and Healthcare; Human-Centred AI

## Transparency in AI

Transparency in AI refers to the degree to which the workings, decisions, and data usage of an AI system can be understood and examined by stakeholders. In health and wellbeing contexts, transparency is essential for **patient trust**, **clinical accountability**, and **regulatory compliance**.

ncy is essential for **patient trust**, **clinical accountability**, and **regulatory compliance**. As defined by the European Parliament, transparency in AI ensures that individuals are made aware when they are communicating or interacting with an AI system, and duly informs deployers of the system's capabilities and limitations.

Transparency is a prerequisite for accountability and is mandated in the EU AI Act for high-risk AI systems, which includes most health-related AI applications.

ted in the EU AI Act for high-risk AI systems, which includes most health-related AI applications.

**Related concepts:** Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI); AI Ethics in Healthcare; Clinical Decision Support; Privacy and Data Governance in Health

## Human-Centred AI

Human-Centred AI (HCAI) is an approach to AI design that focuses on understanding purposes, human values, and desired AI properties in the creation of AI systems.

s on understanding purposes, human values, and desired AI properties in the creation of AI systems. In health and wellbeing systems, HCAI emphasises that AI tools should **augment clinician capabilities** and **empower patients** while maintaining **human oversight** throughout the care process. It draws on principles from **human-computer interaction (HCI)**, **participatory design**, and **cognitive science**, ensuring that technology serves to enhance individual autonomy and quality of life.

ive science**, ensuring that technology serves to enhance individual autonomy and quality of life.

microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi) living in and on the human body, particularly in the gut. ## Automatic Fall Detection

Automatic Fall Detection refers to the use of **sensor-based systems** and **AI algorithms** to detect falls in real time, particularly among **older adults** and individuals with **mobility impairments** or **neurological conditions**. Falls are a leading cause of injury, hospitalisation, and mortality among the elderly, making automated detection a critical component of **health and wellbeing systems**.

the elderly, making automated detection a critical component of **health and wellbeing systems**.

Detection approaches include **wearable sensors** (accelerometers, gyroscopes, barometers embedded in smartwatches or belt-worn devices), **ambient sensors** (cameras, infrared sensors, floor pressure sensors), and **smartphone-based systems**. AI and machine learning techniques — including **threshold-based classifiers**, **support vector machines**, **random forests**, **convolutional neural networks (CNNs)**, and **recurrent neural networks (RNNs/LSTMs)** — are applied to distinguish falls fr

works (CNNs)**, and **recurrent neural networks (RNNs/LSTMs)** — are applied to distinguish falls from normal activities of daily living (ADLs) with high sensitivity and specificity.

Key challenges include reducing **false positives** (e.g., distinguishing a fall from sitting down quickly), ensuring **real-time responsiveness**, achieving **user acceptance** (especially regarding privacy and wearability), and validating systems with **real-world fall data** rather than simulated falls only.

earability), and validating systems with **real-world fall data** rather than simulated falls only. Integration with **emergency alert systems** and **telecare platforms** enables rapid response when a fall is detected.

## Augmented Reality in Health and Wellbeing

Augmented Reality (AR) is a technology that overlays **digital information** — such as images, text, 3D models, or interactive elements — onto the user's perception of the **real-world environment** in real time. In health and wellbeing systems, AR is increasingly relevant as it enables novel applications in **surgical navigation**, **medical education and training**, **rehabilitation**, **patient engagement**, and **assisted living**.

cal education and training**, **rehabilitation**, **patient engagement**, and **assisted living**.

In **surgical settings**, AR can project anatomical structures, tumour boundaries, or instrument trajectories onto the surgeon's field of view, improving precision and reducing operative risks. In **rehabilitation**, AR-based gamified exercises enhance patient motivation and adherence for motor recovery after stroke or orthopaedic surgery. For **medical education**, AR enables immersive anatomy visualisation and simulation of clinical procedures without risk to patients.

les immersive anatomy visualisation and simulation of clinical procedures without risk to patients. In **elderly care and wellbeing**, AR can support **cognitive training**, **navigation assistance** for visually impaired individuals, and **medication reminders** integrated into the living environment.

AR is relevant to health and wellbeing systems because it sits at the intersection of **AI** (for real-time object recognition, tracking, and scene understanding), **wearable technology** (AR headsets and smart glasses), and **human-computer interaction** — all of which are core components of m

dsets and smart glasses), and **human-computer interaction** — all of which are core components of modern wellbeing systems. As AR devices become lighter and more affordable, their integration into clinical workflows and home-based health interventions is expected to grow.

## Blockchain in Healthcare

Blockchain is a **decentralised, distributed digital ledger** technology that records transactions across a peer-to-peer network of computers so that records cannot be altered retroactively without the consensus of the network. In health and wellbeing systems, blockchain is increasingly recognised as a transformative technology for addressing critical challenges related to **health data security**, **patient privacy**, **interoperability**, and **trust** among healthcare stakeholders.

ecurity**, **patient privacy**, **interoperability**, and **trust** among healthcare stakeholders.

Key healthcare applications of blockchain include: **secure exchange of patient data** across hospitals, diagnostic laboratories, pharmacy firms, and physicians; **electronic health record (EHR) management** with patient-controlled access permissions; **pharmaceutical supply chain traceability** to combat counterfeit drugs; **clinical trial data integrity** ensuring transparency and accountability of research results; **genomics data protection** safeguarding sensitive genetic information; and *

of research results; **genomics data protection** safeguarding sensitive genetic information; and **medical insurance claims processing** through smart contracts that automate verification and reduce fraud.

Blockchain's core properties — **immutability**, **decentralisation**, **transparency**, and **cryptographic security** — make it particularly suited to healthcare, where data manipulation can lead to severe and even dangerous consequences.

y suited to healthcare, where data manipulation can lead to severe and even dangerous consequences. By maintaining an incorruptible, auditable log of all transactions, blockchain helps build trust between patients, clinicians, researchers, and institutions. Patients gain greater control over their personal health information, deciding who can access their records and under what conditions. Furthermore, blockchain facilitates **interoperability** between disparate health information systems, enabling seamless and secure data sharing across organisations and borders.

h information systems, enabling seamless and secure data sharing across organisations and borders.

Challenges to blockchain adoption in healthcare include **scalability** (handling large volumes of health data), **energy consumption**, **regulatory compliance** (e.g., reconciling blockchain's immutability with the GDPR's right to erasure), **standardisation**, and the need for **digital literacy** among healthcare professionals and patients.

ndardisation**, and the need for **digital literacy** among healthcare professionals and patients.

**Related concepts:** Privacy and Data Governance in Health; AI and Healthcare; Digital Health; Health Informatics; Genomics and AI; Clinical Decision Support

## EU AI Act

The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is the first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence adopted by a major jurisdiction.

he first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence adopted by a major jurisdiction. It establishes a **risk-based classification** of AI systems into four categories: **unacceptable risk** (prohibited), **high risk** (subject to strict obligations), **limited risk** (transparency obligations), and **minimal risk** (no specific requirements). The regulation was proposed by the European Commission in April 2021, agreed upon in December 2023, and entered into force in August 2024, with phased implementation through 2027.

in December 2023, and entered into force in August 2024, with phased implementation through 2027.

In health and wellbeing contexts, the EU AI Act is particularly significant because it classifies most **medical AI systems** and **AI-based medical devices** as **high-risk**, requiring conformity assessments, risk management systems, human oversight, data governance, transparency documentation, and post-market monitoring. AI systems used in **clinical decision support**, **diagnostic imaging**, **patient triage**, and **health risk assessment** fall under this category.

*diagnostic imaging**, **patient triage**, and **health risk assessment** fall under this category. The Act also introduces specific requirements for **general-purpose AI models** (including large language models), mandating transparency about training data, energy consumption, and compliance with copyright rules.

## Language Model

A language model is a computational model that learns statistical patterns from large amounts of text data to **predict**, **generate**, and **understand** natural language. Modern language models — particularly **large language models (LLMs)** such as GPT, Claude, Mistral, and LLaMA — are based on **transformer architectures** and are trained on vast corpora of text using self-supervised learning.

transformer architectures** and are trained on vast corpora of text using self-supervised learning. They have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in **text generation**, **question answering**, **summarisation**, **translation**, and **reasoning**.

In health and wellbeing systems, language models are increasingly applied to tasks such as **clinical text processing** (extracting information from electronic health records, discharge summaries, and radiology reports), **medical question answering**, **patient communication** (chatbots for symptom checking and health education), **clinical trial

**, **patient communication** (chatbots for symptom checking and health education), **clinical trial matching**, **biomedical literature mining**, and **medical coding automation**. Specialised models such as **Med-PaLM**, **BioGPT**, and **ClinicalBERT** have been fine-tuned on biomedical and clinical data to improve performance on domain-specific tasks.

Key challenges for language models in healthcare include **hallucination** (generating plausible but factually incorrect information), **bias** in training data that may perpetuate health disparities, **privacy concerns** when models are tra

** in training data that may perpetuate health disparities, **privacy concerns** when models are trained on or process sensitive patient data, **lack of explainability** in model outputs, and the need for rigorous **clinical validation** before deployment in care settings. The EU AI Act classifies general-purpose AI models (including LLMs) under specific transparency and governance requirements.

Conclusions
In this work, a method based on unsupervised vector
quantization techniques for automatic ROI calculation is present-
ed.

based on unsupervised vector
quantization techniques for automatic ROI calculation is present-
ed. Specifically, a three-dimensional Self-Organizing Map is used
to model MRI images selecting ROIs related to a particular
neurological disorder. Images from controls and AD patients are
used to compute tissue differences by means of voxel contrastation.
Subsequently, the MRI space is quantized, computing a number
of prototype vectors from features extracted taking into account
the spatial relationship among voxels, figuring out similar areas
within the difference image.

ount
the spatial relationship among voxels, figuring out similar areas
within the difference image. Additionally, the relative importance
of each cluster is computed by means of the cluster sizes and the
statistical significance of the discriminative power of the voxels that
make up the ROI. The spatial relationship among clusters is also
preserved in the SOM output space due to the SOM’s topology
preserving properties. The method has been assessed by selecting a
set of images from the ADNI [40] database, using the ROIs
automatically computed using the presented approach.

es from the ADNI [40] database, using the ROIs
automatically computed using the presented approach. Moreover,
most relevant ROIs computed across this method, specially in
GM, are compatible with areas that appear in literature as
representative regions of AD such as hippocampus [45,46,52].
The classification results provide average accuracy, sensitivity and
specificity values of up to 90%, 87% and 92%, respectively, for 10
cross-validation folds, while the AUC is 0.92. On the other hand,
our method is capable to distinguish MCI from AD patients up to
83% of accuracy and AUC of 0.84.

state the effectiveness of the proposed method to select relevant

Results and Discussion
The proposed architecture was assessed with a series of systematic experiments. For that pur-
pose, a set of falls and conventional movements (or Activities of Daily Living, ADLs) were sim-
ulated by 4 different volunteers (healthy males, aged between 22 and 29 years and 165 –180 cm
tall with an average weight of 67.5kg) in an indoor scenario (a domestic living room).

165 –180 cm
tall with an average weight of 67.5kg) in an indoor scenario (a domestic living room).
The experimental individuals simulated three types of falls (forward, lateral and backward
falls). On the other hand, ADLs consisted of three categories of ordinary mobility patterns:
walking, standing from sitting (and vice versa) and others (comprising movements such as
making gestures with the arms, turning, running or answering the phone). Experiments were
iterated ten times per subject for every type of fall and ADL and for every considered detection
algorithm.

ten times per subject for every type of fall and ADL and for every considered detection
algorithm. For all the tests the smartwatch was worn on the right wrist while the smartphone
was located within a trouser pocket (next to the thigh of the right leg).

Conclusions
The utilization of the inherent sensing and computing capabilities of Android personal devices,
which are currently omnipresent in the daily life of the citizens, has fostered the deployment of
cost-effective Android-based systems for automatic fall detection.
This paper has described and evaluated a prototype of a wearable fall detection system
which benefits from the joint analysis of the user mobility with two commercial Android
devices: a smartphone and a smartwatch.

Summary
Objectives: To select, present, and summarize the best papers 
published in 2017 in the field of Knowledge Representation and 
Management (KRM).
Methods: A comprehensive and standardized review of the 
medical informatics literature was performed to select the 
most interesting papers of KRM published in 2017, based on a 
PubMed query.

tional Medical Informatics Association (IMIA) Yearbook, the five 
best papers for 2018 demonstrate even further the added-value 
of ontology-based integration approaches for phenotype-geno-
type association mining.

Conclusions: Ontologies are demonstrating their maturity to 
integrate medical data and begin to support clinical practices.

The Greek philosopher and polymath Aristotle gives

least two traditional conditions for attributing responsibil-
ity for an action, the so-called control condition and the 
epistemic condition. So, in the control condition, you are 
responsible if you do it (or have done it), if you are the 
agent of the action, if you have caused the action, if you 
have a sufficient degree of control over the action, but to

attribute a full responsibility, an epistemic condition, as

Aristotle argued in the Nicomachean Ethics that the 
action must have its origin in the agent and that one must 
not be ignorant of what one is doing [5 ].
AI technologies do not meet traditional criteria for full 
moral action (and hence preconditions for responsibility)

agent lacks the preconditions for this: An AI cannot really

Automation bias is the tendency for humans to favor

Abstract:
Background:
Work-related stress is a relevant phenomenon in terms of health and safety at work, as occupational distress has a negative impact on individual
and organisational well-being.

Objective:
This work aims to identify versatile tools that can quickly provide reliable measures of work distress. It analyzes the proposal elaborated by the
“Comitato Unico di Garanzia per le Pari Opportunità, la Valorizzazione del Benessere di chi lavora e contro le Discriminazioni” of Rome, i.e.

tool “Valutazione è prevenzione, Sicurezza è partecipazione”.
Methods:
A study was carried out on a sample of 474 employees of the Neapolitan Judicial Offices, who were given a standardized questionnaire to
investigate the stress, associated with the proposal of the Comitato Unico di Garanzia.
Results:
From the elaboration of the results, it emerges that the conditions of working wellbeing are linked to two main factors related to the perception of

sample of employees of the Court of Naples has shown that

Abstract
Medical data are often tricky to get mined for patterns even by the generally demonstrate d
successful modern methodologies of deep learning. This paper puts forward such a medical
classification task, where patient registers of two of the categories are sometimes hard to be
distinguished because of samples showing characteristics of both labels in turn in several
repetitions of the screening procedure.

repetitions of the screening procedure. To this end, the current research appoints a pre-pro-
cessing clustering step (through self-organizing maps) to group the data based on shape
similarity and relabel it accordingly. Subsequently, a deep learning approach (a tandem of
convolutional and long short-term memory networks) performs the training classification
phase on the ‘cleaned’ samples. The dual methodolog y was applied for the computational
diagnosis of electrooculograph y tests within spino-cerebral ataxia of type 2.

duo brings over the deep learner alone does not stem from significantly higher accuracy
results when the performance is considered for all classes. The major finding of this combi-
nation is that half of the presymptomatic cases were correctly found, in opposition to the
single deep model, where this category was sacrificed by the learner in favor of a good accu-
racy overall.

by the eye movement. In a simplified description, this movement during the examination time
represents a saccade and its behavior is further analyzed by the physician. The test is repeated a

The complexity of this medical problem stems from two sides. The first is that a presymp-
tomatic saccade is only slightly different in shape in comparison to a healthy one. The second
issue appears because all the saccades in a patient register are eventually labeled with the same
class found from a (not specified) number of tests, irrespective of the fact that in many more

same
class found from a (not specified) number of tests, irrespective of the fact that in many more
others the movement appears healthy or, on the contrary, presymptomatic. Both aspects pose
a serious problem for machine learning methodologies that strive to discover the relationship
between shape and diagnosis class. As such, their accuracy of discrimination cannot go beyond
66% [3, 4], no matter the techniques employed.
The present study therefore proposes a solution to this classification task through a com-
bined approach of supervised—unsupervised learning.

(SOM), the training saccades get relabeled in a (weighted) way that is linked more to the simi-
larity of shapes than to some unknown and biased (by other unavailable medical information)
decision.

rity of shapes than to some unknown and biased (by other unavailable medical information)
decision. The relabeled training set is then fed to a DL method and the resulting model will
eventually provide the prediction regarding the diagnosis class of the test registers.

4.2 Deep learning for the classification of regrouped saccades
While LSTM have been constructed to possess a long-short term memory in order to handle
temporal data [31], 1D CNN have recently also proved to be able to model time series within
real-world applications either alone [32] or in combination with the former [33]. Therefore,
the architecture used herein will be another combination of the two deep networks with 1D
CNN being in charge of extracting the features and the LSTM of modeling the time dependen-
cies.

CNN being in charge of extracting the features and the LSTM of modeling the time dependen-
cies. Apart from the theoretical precedent, the reason for this tandem stemmed from the sig-
nificantly poorer results observed during pre-experimentation, when either a LSTM or a CNN
was employed alone.
LSTM are deep networks that were built to capture long-term dependencies in the problem
data. They do so through a chain of repeating modules, each composed of a cell state and three
gate functions interacting with it: the forget gate, the input gate and the output gate.

allow for the temporal information to flow, while some of it gets forgotten and other gets
stored.
CNN, on the other hand, has reached popularity due to its success for image analysis, which
admit a natural 2D representation. It has been however transposed to other types of problems,

6 Conclusions
A SOM model is proposed in the current study with the aim of cleaning the training data. The
necessity for using an unsupervised approach comes from the particularity of the problem that
was being dealt with.

ing an unsupervised approach comes from the particularity of the problem that
was being dealt with. The saccades are organized in registers and the class of each register
establishes the class of the saccades it contains. However, the presymptomatic registers contain
both healthy saccades, and some presymptomatic samples that are more similar to the sick
ones. When using the saccades with the actual classes as given by their registers, the CNN-
LSTM model is misled in the mission of delineating between healthy, presymptomatic and
sick samples.

STM model is misled in the mission of delineating between healthy, presymptomatic and
sick samples. An unsupervised approach like SOM finds characteristics from each class in turn
and forms a map in which the neighbors exhibit similarities. Then, since the data is also unbal-
anced, in order to consider a position on the SOM map as representative for the control class,
the score for this class needs to be four times higher than the one for presymptomatic.

ance that the regions on the SOM map indeed correspond to control saccades since so many
training samples from class healthy were assigned to those positions.
An adequate threshold for the ratio between control and presymptomatic is selected based
on the recall of the healthy and presymptomatic results for the validation registers.

care procedures are provided with the intent of 
doing good for the patient involved; and (iv) 
non-maleficence, e.g., health care procedures 
should not harm the patient involved.

movements are commonly executed during social interactions and are determined
by different mental states that may express different positive or negative behavioral
intent. In this context, the effective recognition of festive or violent intent before the
action execution remains crucial for survival.

The terms “festive” and “violent” can be understood diﬀerently
depending on the context and interpretational meaning. The
debate on whether and how linguistic data are a part of a complex
interpretational structure and how they can be implemented in
the mind of the participants remain largely unknown (Hagoort,
2020; Martin and Baggio, 2020).

design, the two participants are in the second frame of meta-

Abstract. The original problem of group testing consists in the identiﬁcation of defective items in
a collection, by applying tests on groups of items that detect the presence of at least one defective
element in the group. The aim is then to identify all defective items of the collection with as few tests
as possible.

defective the most defective item of the group is. In this setting, we propose a simple non-adaptative
algorithm allowing the detection of all defective items of the collection. Items are put on an n × n grid
and pools are organised as lines, columns and diagonals of this grid.

8. Application to the COVID-19 pandemic and open questions
The application of the present algorithm to PCR testing in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic requires
some adaptations and presents a couple of challenges. It should ﬁrst be noted that the simpliﬁcations we made
in our modelling were quite important. We thus begin by discussing in more details the discrepancies between
the real-world problem and our idealized model.
Finite size of samples.

the real-world problem and our idealized model.
Finite size of samples. In COVID-19 pool testing, the items that are tested are samples taken from
subjects, via nasal swab, saliva sample or other method. If there seems to be usually enough matter to split
the sample into several tests, it will not be possible to make an arbitrary large number of tests on each sample.
Therefore, optimal computations made in Section 5 might be somewhat more relevant.

on each sample.

rather than the maximal, although the fact that this viral load is spread over several orders of magnitudes
negates partially this problem as discussed in the introduction.

Added value of this study  
We analysed clinical data from different cohorts totalling 21 607 COVID-19 patients treated in more than 110 
hospitals in Spain and the USA during three different pandemic waves extending from February 2020 to April 
2021. The new CODOP in-hospital mortality prediction model is based on 11 blood biochemistry parameters 
(representing main biological pathways involved in the pathogenesis of SARS-CoV-2) plus Age, all of them 
commonly measured upon hospitalization.

20 features (18 blood biochemical parameters plus Age and Sex; Supplementary Table 1) routinely measured

parameters plus Age (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Figure 1).

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the availability of resources in hospitals around the world experiences 
significant fluctuations following successive infection waves. Thus, a clinically useful prediction tool needs to 
reckon with these dynamic scenarios for effectively assisting undertriage and overtriage decisions.

reckon with these dynamic scenarios for effectively assisting undertriage and overtriage decisions. 
We developed and validated two subtypes of our predictor, CODOP-Ovt (from overtriage) and CODOP-Unt 
(from undertriage), intending to optimize the triage of patients at high risk of death upon arrival to the hospital 
and after their first blood analysis. CODOP-Ovt maximizes the negative predictive value or the detection of 
high-risk patients (high sensitivity) and it is meant for scenarios where overtriage is possible because hospital 
resources are not the main limitation.

for scenarios where overtriage is possible because hospital 
resources are not the main limitation. On the other side, CODOP-Unt maximizes the positive predictive value by 
trying to avoid the inclusion of false high-risk patients (high specificity) and it might be preferred in pandemic 
conditions when hospital resources are limited and undertriage needs to be considered.

Discussion 
The differential access and the low rates of COVID-19 vaccinations, the emergence of more contagious viral 
variants, and the waning of the immune protection project a longer period of health systems under severe strains 
leading to a bigger number of COVID-19 related deaths, particularly in resource-limited countries.

leading to a bigger number of COVID-19 related deaths, particularly in resource-limited countries. A 
conflagration-like scenario will likely be the final set of the pandemic for many nations.22 As a result of an 
altruistic multicontinental effort, we developed and evaluated CODOP, a machine-learning-based online tool

common clinical manifestation in critical COVID-19 patients is composed of a deregulated immune response 
and a robust inflammatory reaction (known as “hypercytokinemia” or “cytokine storm”), which ultimately leads 
to tissue injury.27 Recent reports show a downregulated type-I interferon response leading to an increase of 
neutrophils in severe COVID-19 patients.28.

conventional movements or Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) based on the analysis of the signals 
captured by transportable inertial sensors. Due to the intrinsic difficulties of training and testing

Falls among elderly are a cause of major concern for health systems. According to the World Health Organization 
(WHO)1, around 646,000 mortal falls occur each year in the world, while 37.3 million falls are severe enough to 
require medical attention. Most of these accidents are suffered by adults older than 65 years.

of adults aged over 65 years reported at least one fall in  20182. As a result of falls, 5 to 11% of older individuals 
experience serious injuries, including hip fractures, subdural hematomas or/and severe tissue or head  injuries3. 
A long lie on the floor after a fall without receiving medical assistance is directly associated to a dramatic increase 
of the mortality rate, hospitalization and care home  admissions4.

sociated to a dramatic increase 
of the mortality rate, hospitalization and care home  admissions4. In this context, it is not surprising that fall 
detection systems (FDSs) built on wearable devices have attracted great interest from the scientific community 
in the field of telemedicine and remote monitoring of biosignals.
In contrast with context-aware and video-based alternatives, systems based on wearables may benefit from 
the widespread popularity and low-cost of these devices, while providing an almost-ubiquitous tracking that 
does not interfere with the privacy of the final users.

of testing these detectors in a real environment with older patients, fall detection algorithms are typically gauged 
with movements generated by a group of experimental subjects.
FDSs are binary pattern recognition systems, trained or designed to discriminate activities of daily living

binary pattern recognition systems, trained or designed to discriminate activities of daily living 
(ADL) from violent or agitated movements that can be identified as falls. Although they can also include other 
types of sensors (such as barometers, magnetometers or heart rate monitors), almost all wearable FDSs proposed 
in the literature base their detection decision on the analysis of the signals captured by accelerometers and, in 
some cases, gyroscopes, which are commonly integrated in the same IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit).

some cases, gyroscopes, which are commonly integrated in the same IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit). In this

which a group of volunteers execute a predefined and structured set of ADLs (climbing stairs, walking, running, 
lying down, etc.) and various types of falls (trips, slips, crashes, collapses, etc.) while transporting an IMU in 
one or more body locations.

on machine learning:
• Impersonal universal models, which employ training data from a set of users that will not test the model.

• Personal models, which only consider training data from the final (test) user. This personalization is achieved

Selection of performance metrics and train‑test split strategy. In order to evaluate the trained 
detectors as binary classifiers, we estimated the sensitivity (Se ) or recall, defined as the proportion of falls -or 
positives- in the test subset that are correctly identified, and specificity (Sp), as the ratio of ADLs which are not 
misinterpreted as falls so that they do not trigger a false alarm.

the ratio of ADLs which are not

(such as the accuracy or F1 score), these metrics are not skewed if the number of existing ADLs and falls in the 
datasets are unbalanced (as is the case of the datasets employed in this study). In addition, in order to describe 
the trade-off between these two statistical measures through a single variable, we also computed the geometric 
mean of Se and Sp ( √Se · Sp ) as a global performance metric.

T o calculate these quality metrics, we applied a fivefold cross validation procedure in which the datasets were 
split into five partitions of the same length. Every model of the classifier was then trained and tested five times. 
In each iteration, a different fold was employed for testing while the other four partitions were merged to form 
the training set (following the typical 80–20 rule).

the other four partitions were merged to form 
the training set (following the typical 80–20 rule). Results obtained during the test phase of each iteration are 
then averaged to generate the final metrics.

Conclusions
Wearable fall detection systems (FDSs) provide a cost-effective and non-invasive method to automatically dis-

all detection systems (FDSs) provide a cost-effective and non-invasive method to automatically dis-
criminate falls from other activities of daily life basing on inertial signals (mainly accelerometry). The most 
effective wearable fall detection systems in the literature are founded on machine learning algorithms that usually 
require a learning phase. This training is usually carried out on movement patterns (emulated falls and ADLs) 
captured from a set of experimental subjects different from the target public of these systems, mainly older adults,

t of experimental subjects different from the target public of these systems, mainly older adults, 
who, for obvious reasons, cannot emulate falls for a final fine-tuning of the classifiers.
However, in the vast majority of studies in the literature, FDSs are evaluated with the same subjects who gen-
erated the training samples. This study has focused on systematically analyzing the performance of a ML-based 
FDS when the characteristics of the individuals used in the test are different from those participants employed 
for the training.

the individuals used in the test are different from those participants employed 
for the training. By using five well-known public datasets, four ML algorithms (with different hyperparameter 
configuration) and two alternatives to select the input feature sets, we investigated the impact of this separation of 
training and testing subjects on the effectiveness of the detectors. In particular, we examined the discrimination 
capability of the classifiers when the training and test subjects are separated based on five criteria: weight, height, 
body mass index, gender and age.

st subjects are separated based on five criteria: weight, height, 
body mass index, gender and age. In all cases, the performance metrics of the classifiers (sensitivity, specificity 
and geometric mean of both parameters) were compared with those obtained for: (1) the (optimal) case in which 
the test and training individuals coincide, (2) the case in which the separation of the subjects in both groups 
(test and training) is randomly executed. The results indicate that this segregation of the experimental subjects 
can cause some losses in the classification process.

this segregation of the experimental subjects 
can cause some losses in the classification process. For most of the used datasets, the underperformance seems 
to be somewhat lower if the tallest and heaviest individuals are not included in the training group, which could 
be justified by the fact that corpulent persons generate confusing acceleration patterns (with larger peaks) when 
they perform ADLs. The impact of gender (if we discount its possible correlation with weight or height) or BMI 
is shown to be of secondary importance.

unt its possible correlation with weight or height) or BMI 
is shown to be of secondary importance. Regarding age, the preliminary results illustrate the difficulty of applying 
detection algorithms to older persons when they have been trained exclusively with young subjects. In any event, 
any conclusion derived from the split of the train and test groups based on an age criterion should be taken with 
great caution since the study is strongly limited by the lack of fall patterns associated with elderly volunteers. 
Just one dataset (SisFall) incorporates falls of subjects over 50 years old.

h elderly volunteers. 
Just one dataset (SisFall) incorporates falls of subjects over 50 years old. In addition, the fact that employed falls 
are actually emulated may also distort the registered divergences between the two groups (younger and older 
participants), as they may be really caused by the differences in the way these two groups emulate a fall accident 
and not by the compensatory movements that they would perform during an actual fall.
In any case, the study discloses that the characteristics of the participants have much less impact on the effec-

he study discloses that the characteristics of the participants have much less impact on the effec-
tiveness of the classifiers than the type of movements used for training and testing. Moreover, the performed 
tests show that the algorithms clearly tend to overlearn the particular ADLs used for training, in such a way that, 
during the test phase, they have difficulties to identify new ADL routines, especially if they involve sudden or 
highly energetic movements (such as sport-type activities), as they are misclassified as falls.

or 
highly energetic movements (such as sport-type activities), as they are misclassified as falls. These results show 
the importance of training the fall detectors with as many activities as possible. In contrast with the procedure 
typically employed by the related literature, the discrimination and extrapolation capability of FDSs should be 
equally tested against a wide variety of ADLs and falls, including movements not present in the training set.

Introduction
Carotid atherosclerotic plaque ulceration and rupture are one of the main causes of major adverse
cardiac events such as ischemic stroke, which account for approximately one-fourth of all strokes (1).
Luminal stenosis degree has been historically considered the most important parameter to grade the

Luminal stenosis degree has been historically considered the most important parameter to grade the
severity of atherosclerotic disease and risk-stratify patients and treatment decision-making (2). However,
new pathological studies have demonstrated major differences in the composition and risk of rupture for
plaques with identical degrees of stenosis (3). The technological advancement of vascular imaging
techniques such as CT and MR angiography allowed a routine high-resolution characterization of carotid
plaque features.

Discussion
In this study, we proposed a proof of concept of a machine-learning model that classify fertile and infertile cou-
ples according to anthropometric, antioxidative, and metabolic signatures.

rtile and infertile cou-
ples according to anthropometric, antioxidative, and metabolic signatures. Besides of thoroughly documented 
causes of infertility such as genetic, congenital, and acquired defects, increasing interest should also be focused 
on the environmental and lifestyle  factors21. Indeed, addictions to tobacco, alcohol, and drugs, as well as diet, 
physical activity, obesity, metabolic disorders, sleep, and stress, also compromise male and female  fertility5,18,34–37. 
Interestingly, the impact of these factors is reversible if apropriate corrective measures are taken.

factors are commonly studied separatly, while their effects may be cumulative in  combination38. Therefore, it 
seemed helpful to build a model including the several lifestyle-related factors as well as the two members of the 
couple to quantitatively predict the infertility degrees.

Conclusion
The proposed model is a multivariate supervised statistical model built from data drawn from infertile men and 
women who are considered as a unique couple in observation.

in discriminatory power compared to models in which analysis of men or women are implemented separately.
The proposed model could find its place in the standard care management of couples with parental project. 
This approach is interesting since personalized lifestyle intervention should be considered as a first-choice treat-
ment for idiopathic infertility and should be systematicaly suggested before ART.

Abstract 
Background: Within a few months, the COVID-19 pandemic has spread to many 
countries and has been a real challenge for health systems all around the world. This 
unprecedented crisis has led to a surge of online discussions about potential cures for the 
disease. Among them, vaccines have been at the heart of the debates, and have faced lack 
of confidence before marketing in France. 
Objective: This study aims to identify and investigate the opinion of French Twitter 
users on the announced vaccines against COVID-19 through sentiment analysis.

Methods: This study was conducted in two phases. First, we filtered a collection of 
tweets related to COVID-19 from February to August 2020 with a set of keywords 
associated with vaccine mistrust using word embeddings. Second, we performed 
sentiment analysis using deep learning to identify the characteristics of vaccine mistrust. 
The model was trained on a hand labeled subset of 4,548 tweets.

results presented in the rest of this paper concern the 344k French tweets related to a 
potential vaccine against COVID-19.

Conclusions 
Our study showed that Twitter could be a useful tool to investigate the arguments of 
vaccine mistrust. Our results unveil that political aspects of vaccination overshadow its 
usual criticisms about adverse drug reactions.

more homogenous and more widely spread than the positive rhetoric, we believe that this 
study provides effective tools to help health authorities better understand vaccine 
mistrust.

Summary
Objectives: To summarize recent research and select the best papers 
published in 2016 in the field of computerized clinical decision sup-
port for the Decision Support section of the IMIA yearbook.
Methods: A literature review was performed by searching two 
bibliographic databases for papers related to clinical decision 
support systems (CDSSs). The aim was to identify a list of 
candidate best papers from the retrieved papers that were then 
peer-reviewed by external reviewers.

the IMIA editorial team finally selected the best papers on the 
basis of all reviews and section editor evaluation.
Results: Among the 1,145 retrieved papers, the entire review process 
resulted in the selection of four best papers. The first paper describes 
machine learning models used to predict breast cancer multidisci-
plinary team decisions and compares them with two predictors based 
on guideline knowledge.

therapy, i.e. after surgery was completed. 
At this step of the patient management,

ries, chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, and 
targeted therapy, and for each category, the 
outcome can be recommended, non-recom-
mended, or discussable.

Discussion
Recent studies have shown that DL language models based on the transformer  architecture9, such as the GPT-2, 
have remarkable performances in explaining the neural correlates of language comprehension and likely share 
some computational principles with the human  brain4–6,15.

language comprehension and likely share 
some computational principles with the human  brain4–6,15. In this work, we provided further support to this 
hypothesis, and contributed some novel insights about two basic neural mechanisms underpinning language 
comprehension in humans: word prediction and context-related language processing.
The contribution of this research is two-fold: first our results illustrate with a novel methodology how it is 
possible to expose an attention-based neural network and a group of human listeners to the same narrative

In particular, our results corroborate the idea that word-level prediction is accurately indexed by the surprisal

as the GPT-2, rather than using a stochastic language model.

Conclusions
In this work, the neural correlates of narrative comprehension in a naturalistic fMRI experiment have been 
mapped with two metrics estimated with a state-of-art DL language model (GPT-2): the surprisal and the sali -
ency scores. The results observed in the surprisal analysis confirm previous studies and further support the use 
of DL language models to explain the fMRI signal during spoken narrative listening.

upport the use 
of DL language models to explain the fMRI signal during spoken narrative listening. The analysis of the sali-
ency scores revealed the presence of a weighing mechanism operating on the listened words which takes place 
in the superior and middle temporal cortex. As this mechanism explains the performance of an NLP tool in 
the prediction of new words from the current segment of text, this finding establishes a novel link between the 
ways the human brain and the chosen DL language model (GPT-2) build up inferences about the next incoming 
word.

n brain and the chosen DL language model (GPT-2) build up inferences about the next incoming 
word. This approach works by unpacking the internal reasoning approach of the artificial neural network and, 
despite the architectural differences, seems to feature a similar mechanism of neural processing in the brain 
which may inspire novel strategies for addressing human performances in complex cognitive tasks, including 
natural language comprehension.

Summary
Objectives: To introduce the 2022 International Medical Infor-
matics Association (IMIA) Yearbook by the editors.
Methods: The editorial provides an introduction and overview to 
the 2022 IMIA Yearbook whose special topic is “Inclusive Digital 
Health: Addressing Equity, Literacy, and Bias for Resilient Health 
Systems”. The special topic, survey papers, section editor synop-
ses and some best papers are discussed.

s”. The special topic, survey papers, section editor synop-
ses and some best papers are discussed. The sections’ changes in 
the Yearbook Editorial Committee are also described.
Results: As shown in the previous edition, health informatics in 
the context of a global pandemic has led to the development of 
ways to collect, standardize, disseminate and reuse data world-
wide. The Corona Virus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has 
demonstrated the need for timely, reliable, open, and globally 
available information to support decision making.

he need for timely, reliable, open, and globally 
available information to support decision making. It has also 
highlighted the need to address social inequities and disparities 
in access to care across communities. This edition of the Yearbook 
acknowledges the fact that much work has been done to study 
health equity in recent years in the various fields of health 
informatics research. 
Conclusion: There is a strong desire to better consider disparities 
between populations to avoid biases being induced in Artificial 
Intelligence algorithms in particular.

een populations to avoid biases being induced in Artificial 
Intelligence algorithms in particular. Telemedicine and m-health 
must be more inclusive for people with disabilities or living in 
isolated geographical areas.

1. Introduction
Medical imaging play a crucial role in the clinical practice worldwide. As a
non-invasive technique, they provide crucial information for the diagnosis of a
wide range of diseases. Despite the high spatial resolution that current medical
imaging provide, performing a correct diagnosis is not a straightforward task.
Success depends on factors such as the expertise of the doctors or the overlap-
ping between symptoms associated with similar pathologies. This leads to a
manual, time-consuming process that may delay diagnosis and the election of a
correct treatment.

[1, 2, 3], whereas others have been successfully employed in the classiﬁcation
stage [4, 5, 6]. The emergence of deep neural networks has revolutionized the
automatic classiﬁcation of medical images.

3.3. Ensemble Classiﬁcation
The development of a CAD (Computer-aided diagnosis) system for the de-
tection of a certain disease relies on the assumption that patterns associated
with this pathology are similar among patients. However, the signs and symp-
toms may diﬀer depending on the virulence of the disease.

ng patients. However, the signs and symp-
toms may diﬀer depending on the virulence of the disease. The presence of
other abnormal ﬁndings that are not related to the disorder can also aﬀect the
reliability of the classiﬁcation system, in addition to the artifacts during the
acquisition of the images. To overcome these potential pitfalls, we propose an
ensemble framework in which diﬀerent classiﬁers analyze local regions of the
images. Afterwards, the decisions of each classiﬁer are combined according to
the reliability of each classiﬁer’s prediction.

divided into cubic patches [41]. For each individual patch, kernel PCA is ap-
plied, entering the resulting components into the classiﬁer. The number (and
hence, size) of the patches were selected in order to match the potential size of
the informative patterns, guaranteeing to strike a balance between performance
and computational cost.

6. Discussion
In this study, an image classiﬁcation framework based on a probabilistic
combination of classiﬁers is proposed. This approach relies on a scheme in which
each image is divided into diﬀerent patches.

each image is divided into diﬀerent patches. From each one of them, features
are extracted by using kernel PCA, and classiﬁcation is then performed through
a probabilistic RBF-SVM classiﬁer. The outputs of individual classiﬁers are
combined in an ensemble according to the reliability of their predictions. We
evaluated the performance of this approach in terms of diﬀerent measures and
studied the inﬂuence of the patches size in the global performance and the
relationship between individual and global decisions.

extremely important that a simple method like kernel PCA was able to extract
the relevant information from each patch.

To furnish  explainability4, we resort to a visualisation considering activation maps, typically exploited for 
deep learning network debug. For this purpose, we resort to the Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping 
(Grad-CAM)  algorithm34.
The Grad-CAM is a technique to extract the gradients of the DL models convolutional layers and use them 
to provide graphical information on the inference step.

L models convolutional layers and use them 
to provide graphical information on the inference step. Briefly, the gradients capture high-level visual patterns 
and can describe which areas of the input image have influenced the most the model output decision. Also, the 
convolutional layer preserves spatial information, thus, the Grad-CAM uses this data to provide a heatmap of 
the input image. This heatmap highlights the input image area which was used by the DL model to classify a 
specific input; it provides a visual “explanation” to a certain decision.

e DL model to classify a 
specific input; it provides a visual “explanation” to a certain decision. The Grad-CAM adopted in this work is an 
implementation of the one introduced by this  paper34.
Simply put, Grad-CAM uses the gradients of any target concept, flowing into the final convolutional layer to 
produce a coarse location map that highlights the important regions in the image to predict the concept.

Grad-CAM works by observing the last network convolutional layer and then examining the gradient infor-

Conclusion and future work
We design an approach focused on the detection of covid-19 by analysing CT medical images. In particular, we 
consider a transfer learning model developed by authors, aimed to label a CT as covid-19 , for patients affected 
with the covid-19; other, for patients affected with a pulmonary disease different from the covid-19 one; and 
healthy, for patients with no pulmonary disease.

healthy, for patients with no pulmonary disease. As additional contribution, the proposed approach is aimed 
to highlight on the patient CT the areas symptomatic of the infection provided by covid-19: this represents an 
important characteristic because this representation can provide interesting and useful information to pathologist 
and radiologist.

and radiologist. We think that the proposed method can be considered for a rapid screening and for an immedi-
ate diagnosis and visualisation of the lung areas affected by the covid-19 infection.

Introduction
Over the past decade, immunotherapy (IO) has signi ﬁcantly
changed the therapeutic landscape of lung cancer, particularly
non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ( 1, 2). The median overall
survival (mOS) of patients w ith advanced non-oncogene
addicted NSCLC improved from approximately 12 months in
the chemotherapy era to about 24 months with the advent of IO
(3).

from approximately 12 months in
the chemotherapy era to about 24 months with the advent of IO
(3). The 5-year survival rate increased from 16% with
chemotherapy alone to 32% with the addition of IO ( 4).
Despite these important results, only 30-50% of patients
achieve long-term bene ﬁts from IO ( 5–7).
In clinical practice, Programmed Death-Ligand 1 (PD-L1) is as
of now the only biomarker used to predict response to ICIs as a
higher PD-L1 expression is generallyassociated with the possibility
of response to IO.
